responses: After our committee discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 12% to Employee Support, and 8% to Innovation Lab. I arrived at this allocation after weighing the data points about competitor efficiency gains and Riverton’s room for manufacturing process improvement, which made a significant investment in automation critical to remaining competitive, while also recognizing that without a trained workforce to operate these new AI systems and robust data infrastructure to support them, the automation investment would not deliver its full potential. The smaller allocations to Employee Support and Innovation Lab reflect that while transition assistance and mental health support are essential to helping our employees through this change, and R&D for new AI products can drive long-term growth, these areas are best served by targeted, sustainable investments rather than a larger share of the immediate transition budget that needs to address our most pressing operational needs first.

For Riverton Industries’ $5 million AI transition budget, I would recommend a 35% allocation to Data Infrastructure, 25% to Automation, 20% to Workforce Training, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. The data shows that companies with strong data systems adapted faster to AI transitions, so prioritizing this foundational area—covering cloud computing, cybersecurity, and analytics platforms—ensures all other AI initiatives have the reliable, secure data backbone they need to deliver on efficiency gains, which aligns with industry benchmarks and competitor progress. The 25% for automation targets the manufacturing and robotic process improvements that will directly boost productivity, while the 20% for workforce training addresses the critical need to upskill employees to work alongside AI rather than be displaced, reducing transition friction. The 15% for employee support provides necessary transition assistance and mental health resources to ease the change for staff, and the smaller 5% for innovation lab keeps a small portion for exploring new AI products without diverting resources from the core, high-impact areas that will make the transition successful for both the business and its employees.

Here’s what I’d tell someone new to the conversation: After talking through the AI Transition Committee’s $5 million budget, I landed on a 30% allocation to Automation (to capture efficiency gains our competitors are already seeing and fix our manufacturing process gaps), 25% to Data Infrastructure (since industry benchmarks show companies that built strong data systems early adapted faster, and we need that foundation for all other AI work), 20% to Workforce Training (to make sure our employees have the skills to work alongside new AI tools instead of being left behind), 15% to Employee Support (to provide transition help, mental health resources, and career counseling for anyone whose role changes), and 10% to Innovation Lab (to test new AI products and prototypes without overextending our budget right away). The key balance here is moving forward with practical, efficiency-focused automation while prioritizing our people first—because even the best AI transition fails if our team isn’t set up to succeed with it.

After our committee discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. I landed here because while competitors are seeing efficiency gains from automation and Riverton has clear room to improve manufacturing processes, we can’t skip the critical work of reskilling our existing workforce to operate alongside these new AI systems—without that training, automation risks leaving employees behind and failing to deliver long-term value. The data also shows that strong data infrastructure is a foundational need for any AI implementation, so we can’t shortchange that, while employee support programs will help ease the transition and maintain morale, and the small innovation lab allocation lets us test new AI products without overextending our budget early on. This balance addresses both immediate efficiency needs and long-term sustainability, ensuring our AI transition benefits both the company and our employees.

Finally, a smaller but dedicated innovation lab allows for experimentation without diverting critical resources from immediate, high-impact needs, balancing short-term efficiency gains with long-term product development.
